title: Heart Failure
path: Nursing Care of Patients with Cardiovascular Disorders

headings.title: Understanding Heart Failure: An Overview
headings.content: Heart failure is a clinical syndrome where the heart muscle fails to pump blood effectively enough to meet the body's metabolic needs. It does not mean the heart has stopped working entirely, but rather that its pumping efficiency is compromised. In obstetric and general medical practice, midwives frequently encounter this condition either as a pre-existing chronic illness or as a new complication brought on by the immense hemodynamic demands of pregnancy. When the heart cannot keep up, blood and fluid back up into the lungs or body tissues, leading to congestion and restricted tissue perfusion. Understanding this fundamental failure of the cardiac pump helps explain the diverse symptoms patients experience.

headings.title: Pathophysiology and Compensatory Mechanisms
headings.content:
When cardiac output drops, the body activates several compensatory mechanisms to maintain perfusion to vital organs like the brain and kidneys. While these responses help in the short term, they ultimately worsen the heart failure over time.

- **Sympathetic Nervous System Activation**: Releases adrenaline and noradrenaline to increase heart rate and force of contraction, which increases myocardial workload.
- **Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS)**: Reduced blood flow to the kidneys triggers renin release, causing vasoconstriction and sodium and water retention to expand blood volume.
- **Myocardial Remodeling**: The heart chambers change shape, dilate, or thicken in an attempt to handle the workload, which eventually makes the muscle weaker and less efficient.

headings.title: Clinical Manifestations
headings.content:
The clinical presentation of heart failure depends on whether the left side, the right side, or both sides of the heart are failing. Left-sided heart failure primarily causes pulmonary congestion because blood backs up into the lungs. Right-sided heart failure causes systemic venous congestion, leading to fluid accumulation in the body.

| Side of Heart | Primary Clinical Signs and Symptoms | Common Causes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Left-Sided | Dyspnea, orthopnea, crackles in lung bases, cough with pink frothy sputum | Hypertension, myocardial infarction |
| Right-Sided | Peripheral pitting edema, jugular venous distension, ascites, hepatomegaly | Left-sided failure, pulmonary hypertension |

headings.title: Diagnostic Evaluation
headings.content:
Diagnosing heart failure involves a combination of clinical assessment, laboratory tests, and imaging studies. A thorough history and physical examination help identify risk factors and physical signs of fluid overload. 

Blood tests play a crucial role, particularly the measurement of **natriuretic peptides** (such as BNP or NT-proBNP). These hormones are released by stretched heart muscle cells, making them reliable markers for heart failure severity. An **electrocardiogram (ECG)** checks for arrhythmias, ischemia, or structural enlargement. The gold standard imaging tool is the **echocardiogram**, which visualizes heart valves, measures chamber sizes, and calculates the ejection fraction to determine how well the heart pumps blood.

headings.title: Medical Management and Pharmacotherapy
headings.content: Pharmacological treatment aims to reduce cardiac workload, control fluid retention, and improve overall survival. Commonly prescribed medication classes include diuretics, which relieve congestion by prompting the kidneys to excrete excess salt and water. ACE inhibitors or ARBs relax blood vessels, lower blood pressure, and slow down detrimental heart remodeling. Beta-blockers slow the heart rate and reduce myocardial oxygen demand over the long term. In specific cases, digitalis glycosides like digoxin are used to strengthen the force of myocardial contraction while slowing the heart rate.

headings.title: Nursing Care and Interventions
headings.content: Midwives and nurses caring for patients with heart failure must focus on meticulous monitoring and supportive care. Vital signs should be checked regularly, with close attention paid to respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, and blood pressure. Accurate fluid balance charting is essential, requiring daily weight measurements at the same time each day using the same scale. A sudden weight gain of over one kilogram within a couple of days usually signals fluid retention. Positioning the patient upright with legs dependent helps ease breathing by reducing venous return to the chest. Administering prescribed oxygen therapy maintains adequate tissue oxygenation during acute episodes.

headings.title: Special Considerations in Pregnancy
headings.content: Pregnancy induces profound physiological changes, including a 30 to 50 percent increase in blood volume and cardiac output. For a compromised heart, this added workload can trigger acute decompensation. Midwives must remain vigilant for signs of peripartum cardiomyopathy, a form of heart failure that develops toward the end of pregnancy or in the months following delivery. Multidisciplinary care involving obstetricians and cardiologists is vital. Labor and delivery require careful hemodynamic monitoring, pain relief to minimize stress, and careful fluid management to prevent postpartum pulmonary edema.

headings.title: Patient Education and Lifestyle Modification
headings.content: Empowering patients and their families with practical knowledge is vital for preventing frequent hospital readmissions. Midwives should educate patients on dietary sodium restriction, as salt promotes fluid retention. Fluid intake limits may also be prescribed in severe cases. Patients must learn to recognize warning signs that require immediate medical attention, such as worsening shortness of breath, rapid weight gain, persistent cough, or severe swelling. Encouraging adherence to prescribed medication regimens and scheduled follow-up visits ensures long-term stability and a better quality of life.
